REPLY BRIEF OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC 
Constellation submits this reply brief1 to address four issues. First, we urge the 
Commission to reject PJM’s proposal to delay by three years–until June 2029,2 beyond the second 
Trump Administration–the implementation of Interim Network Integration Transmission Service 
(“Interim NITS”). There is no good reason for such a delay, which will only harm PJM’s ability 
to timely interconnect new data center load while any needed transmission upgrades are being 
constructed. Urgency, not delay, is needed. The Commission should therefore establish a separate 
track to promptly approve the rates and terms for Interim NITS as modified below and make them 
effective no later than October 1, 2026.3 Urgency was a principal motivation for the Commission’s

REPLY 
I. 
The Commission Should Fast Track Interim NITS  
The fastest approach to “release the bottleneck of large load investments across the PJM 
footprint”25 and obtain national and economic security is to quickly implement Interim NITS for 
new and pending large load applicants. Taking three and half years to implement this transmission 
service will not win the AI race, and such delay is inconsistent with the Commission’s 
December 18th Order.26 Immediately after the paper hearing briefing concludes, the Commission 
should establish a separate track to promptly approve the rates and terms for Interim NITS as 
modified below in Section III and make them effective no later than October 1, 2026. 
Five months is a reasonable amount of time to implement this service and advance the 
Commission’s goal of speedy interconnection. Indeed, PJM itself has been working on such a 
service since at least March 2025 when it suggested its “Option 7” in its Answer to the 
February 2025 Show Cause Order.27 Underscoring that there is no barrier to timely 
implementation, the Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”) recently committed to making its version of 
Interim NITS, Conditional High Impact Large Loads Service (“CHILLS”), available on July 1 of 
this year, less than five months after filing its revised tariff proposing the service and less than 
three months after SPP’s requested action date by the Commission.28 PJM should be expected to 
act with comparable urgency.

PJM offers no legitimate reason for proposing a three and half year delay. PJM first claims 
that Interim NITS “will significantly affect the PJM Load Forecast and expected demand.”29 This 
is incorrect. The point of Interim NITS, as the Commission recognized, is that Co-Located Loads 
served by Interim NITS are “interruptible loads” and “capacity will not be procured on their behalf 
until such time as the Network Upgrades are in place to serve them.”30 PJM has not explained how 
Interim NITS will impact its load forecast.  
PJM next claims that the service should be delayed by more than three years because “the 
addition of the three new transmission services will require significant changes to PJM’s core 
Markets and Operations systems”31 as they do not currently “automate Curtailment of Non-Firm 
Contract Demand Transmission Service (or Interim NITS) before Firm Contract Demand 
Transmission Service.”32 PJM implies implementing these changes could be delayed by “vendor 
availability, the speed with which the system changes can be designed, and the interaction of these 
requested changes with other competing priorities.”33 Possible logistical challenges will not risk 
delay if the Commission separates and implements Interim NITS on a fast track. Like SPP, PJM 
will only need to automate curtailment of Interim NITS before NITS just as it does for external 
Non-Firm Point to Point Transmission Service. Before entering Emergency Procedures, “PJM

II. 
PJM Proposes to Restrict Contract Demand Services in Conflict with the December 18th 
Order 
PJM proposes to restrict Contract Demand Services in two ways: first, by restricting Non-
Firm Contract Demand Service to a Co-Located Generating Facility’s outage,44 and second, by 
requiring Firm Contract Demand Service for any portion of the Co-Located Load not served by 
the Co-Located Generating Facility.45 These restrictions contradict or are otherwise inconsistent 
with the December 18th Order. They should be rejected.  
First, the Commission did not limit Eligible Customers to taking Non-Firm Contract 
Demand Service only at times when the Co-Located Generating Facility is on outage. The 
December 18th Order made Non-Firm Contract Demand Service available for Eligible Customers

III. 
The Commission Should Encourage Its New Transmission Services and Reject Attempts 
that Frustrate Their Use 
PJM and Indicated Transmission Owners propose provisions that would restrict, delay or

inherently shrinks the quantity of costs that could be customer-classified and makes 
12 
the need to perform this step less important. Additionally, transmission 
13 
customers—whether large individual loads or aggregations of smaller loads—have 
14 
traditionally imposed a meaningful level of demand on the system, meaning there 
15 
has not been a significant need to allocate a portion of transmission system costs to 
16 
customers that are not actually drawing power from the grid. Against this backdrop, 
17 
utilities typically allocate transmission costs largely on the basis of demand. In 
18 
effect, this classifies 0% of transmission costs to the “customer” cost driver.

Q24. IS THE MINIMUM SYSTEM METHOD APPROPRIATE IN THE 
1 
CONTEXT OF THE GRC AND WHY? 
2 
A24. Yes. While the minimum system method is typically not used in the context of 
3 
transmission cost allocation or ratemaking, the cost of the minimum system is 
4 
precisely the set of costs that a co-located load that benefits from the existence of 
5 
wires but imposes no demand on the grid should share. The costs of the minimum 
6 
system therefore provide a theoretically-sound basis to calculate the GRC. 
7 
Q25. HOW CAN THE RESULTS OF A MINIMUM SYSTEM STUDY BE USED 
8 
TO ESTIMATE THE GRC? 
9 
A25. A transmission minimum system study could estimate the customer-driven share of 
10 
transmission costs as a fraction of the total PJM transmission revenue requirement. 
11 
This fraction could then be applied to each PJM Transmission Owner’s Network 
12 
Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”) rate to estimate the GRC in dollars per 
13 
kW-year. For example, if the minimum system study indicates that 5% of 
14 
transmission costs are customer-driven, the GRC would be 5% of the applicable 
15 
NITS rate. 
16 
Q26. WHAT RANGES DO MINIMUM SYSTEM STUDIES GENERALLY 
17 
YIELD FOR THE FRACTION OF COSTS THAT ARE CUSTOMER-
18 
DRIVEN? 
19 
A26. As stated previously, utilities typically only use the minimum system method to 
20 
classify distribution costs, not transmission costs, to the “customer” cost driver. 
21 
While these results vary by utility, a typical range of results may show that between 
22

18 
30% – 50% of distribution costs are driven by the number of customers on the 
1 
system. For example, a recent filing from PPL shows that 43% of distribution costs 
2 
were categorized to the customer category using the minimum system method.24 
3 
Q27. HOW WOULD THESE RESULTS CHANGE IF APPLIED TO THE 
4 
TRANSMISSION SYSTEM INSTEAD OF THE DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM? 
5 
A27. Applying the minimum system method to the transmission system would 
6 
definitionally yield a smaller fraction than the distribution-level values discussed 
7 
above. This is because transmission system components are much larger than 
8 
distribution system components, so the minimum system is a smaller fraction of 
9 
total transmission system costs. 
10 
As discussed above, no utilities that I am aware of classify any transmission 
11 
costs to the customer cost driver, meaning they are implicitly assuming a minimum 
12 
system value of 0% for the transmission system. Thus, it is reasonable to assume 
13 
that a proper minimum system study when applied to the transmission system 
14 
would yield a value significantly lower than 25.8%. 
15

VALUE BE CALCULATED FOR APPLICATION TO THE GRC? 
2 
A29. While the results of my calculation above are reasonable, they are based on

relatively high-level publicly available data. For specific application to the GRC, 
4 
the Transmission Owners should perform a minimum system study for the PJM 
5 
transmission system using more detailed information about their system. 
6 
Q30. HOW WOULD YOU ASSESS WHETHER THE RESULTS OF ANY PJM-
7 
SPECIFIC MINIMUM SYSTEM STUDY ARE REASONABLE? 
8 
A30. As discussed above, there is little to no precedent for applying the minimum system 
9 
method to the transmission system, so there is relatively little available data upon 
10 
which to benchmark results. Nonetheless, it is the case that most utilities implicitly 
11 
classify transmission costs 100% to demand and 0% to customer. This implicitly 
12 
means that something significantly lower than the 25.8% charge proposed by the 
13 
Transmission Owners. It is also definitionally true that applying the minimum 
14 
system to the transmission system should yield a smaller fraction than if applying 
15 
it to the distribution system. 
16 
Based on this information and my calculation estimate above, a minimum 
17 
system that yields between 2% to 10% of actual system costs is reasonable based 
18 
on the sheer differences of minimum components relative to the large towers and 
19 
conductors that constitute the PJM system. Any result higher than 10% would be 
20 
unreasonable and should call into question the methodological approach or 
21 
assumptions used in the study, with demand-driven transmission costs likely being 
22 
improperly assigned to customers that do not cause them.  
23

22 
Q31. HOW SHOULD THE OUTPUT OF A MINIMUM SYSTEM STUDY BE 
1 
USED TO CALCULATE THE GRC? 
2 
A31. The minimum system study will yield a percentage value that is substitutable for 
3 
(but lower than) the 25.8% value that the Transmission Owners have proposed as 
4 
their Grid Reliance Percentage Allocator to calculate the GRC. The only difference 
5 
is that a value calculated using the minimum system that is below 10% will be both 
6 
theoretically sound, fair, just, and reasonable. With a new and lower Grid Reliance 
7 
Percentage Allocator, the Transmission Owners should re-calculate the GRC using 
8 
the same methodology that they have already proposed. 
9 
Q32. WHAT ARE THE IMPACTS OF A GRC THAT IS TOO HIGH? 
10 
A32. Customers that pay the GRC by definition do not impose any incremental cost on 
11 
the transmission system. Thus, all GRC charges that the Transmission Owners 
12 
collect are used to directly reduce the NITS rate for all other customers.28 In this 
13 
regard, it may seem that a higher GRC rate would yield higher GRC revenues and 
14 
thus higher reductions to the NITS rate for all other customers. However, basic 
15 
economics tells us that this is not necessarily the case. As Art Laffer artfully 
16 
demonstrated, higher tax rates can actually yield lower tax revenues to the extent 
17 
that they discourage work and investment.29  
18 
In the case of the GRC, inappropriately increasing the rate to too high of a 
19 
level could have the effect of reducing absolute GRC revenues for two reasons. 
20 
First, it could discourage the development of co-located load in the PJM region. 
21

Second, it could disincentivize the configuration of load in a lower cost co-located 
1 
configuration and instead incentivize configuration of load in a higher cost NITS 
2 
configuration that would require inefficient buildout of the transmission system. An 
3 
explicit objective of this proceeding is to “avoid costly and inefficient transmission 
4 
system buildout that may not be necessary.”30 Thus, a GRC that is too high risks 
5 
inefficiently increasing system costs and reducing GRC collections that can be used 
6 
to reduce the NITS rate for other customers. It is therefore not in the best interest 
7 
of PJM’s consumers for Transmission Owners to seek a high GRC that would 
8 
ultimately reduce GRC revenue collections.

5 Recommendations & Summary 
1 
Q33. IN LIGHT OF THE ARGUMENTS YOU MAKE, DO YOU HAVE A 
2 
RECOMMENDATION? 
3 
A33. Yes. I recommend that FERC not approve either the methodology or value for the 
4 
Grid Reliance Charge (“GRC”) that the Transmission Owners have put forward. It 
5 
is not theoretically sound, has no precedent, and is unreasonably high. Instead, I 
6 
recommend that FERC order PJM to conduct a minimum system study to determine 
7 
a percentage that can be applied to the NITS rate to calculate the GRC. I estimate 
8 
that 6% of NITS is a reasonable basis for the GRC, but any value between 2% to 
9 
10% may be reasonable. FERC should ensure that PJM does not produce a GRC 
10 
rate higher than 10% of the NITS rate which would be unreasonable, not aligned 
11 
with cost causation principles, and would call into question the methodological 
12 
approach or assumptions.  
13 
Q34. PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR TESTIMONY. 
14 
A34. Yes. The key takeaways of my testimony are: 
15 
• The concept of a GRC is reasonable so that co-located loads make some 
16 
contribution to the cost of the wires that deliver the ancillary services they 
17 
consume; 
18 
• The Transmission Owners’ proposal for the GRC is unjust and unreasonable 
19 
because it is not based on sound ratemaking principles, has no precedent, is 
20 
inconsistent with cost causation principles, and is unreasonably high; 
21

25 
• The minimum system method provides a theoretically sound basis for 
1 
developing a GRC; 
2 
• Using the minimum system method, I estimate an appropriate GRC should be 
3 
6% of the NITS rate, although a value between 2% to 10% may be reasonable; 
4 
and 
5 
• A GRC rate that is too high could have the unintended negative consequences 
6 
of both reducing GRC revenues and causing inefficient transmission buildout, 
7 
contrary to the objective of the FERC Order. 
8

9
